thesis.claim: A raider that breeds as the world's own agents can takes hold where the barren raider could not, and it is the raid that does it. In B2's worlds played on, at iterations 5,000 and 10,000, where patches of 5% of Chapter 51's raider, which has a child only when it holds 30 tokens, took hold in none of 30 plantings, patches of 5% of a raider that has a child of ten tokens whenever it holds more take hold in at least 5 of the same 30, and in more of them than patches of a turtle that breeds the same way but never raids.
thesis.why: In Experiment 33 neither kind of raider had a child: of the 7,587 agents the patches were planted on, 4 held the 30 tokens their rules wait for. A barren patch lives only as long as the nodes it holds and the nodes it takes, and in B2 every agent dies at age 100; the crews died with the youngest agent they were planted on. The world's own agents have a child as soon as they can give it ten tokens (B2's min_child). A raider that does the same replaces its dead, and each of its children can raid at once: seven tokens staked take a stranger of up to four. The breeding turtle breeds the same way and never raids, and so tells breeding alone from breeding and raiding.
thesis.confirm: Breeding raiders take hold in at least 5 of the 30 plantings at 5,000 and 10,000, and in more of them than breeding turtles do: alive after 300 iterations, more than the patch began with, and more than the control planted in the same place.
thesis.refute: Breeding raiders take hold in 4 or fewer of the 30, or in no more of them than breeding turtles: breeding does not open the door, or the raid adds nothing to it; the chapter says which.
